articles.summary: Nvidia’s board is preparing to remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reports, three days after the same board said it trusted
articles.body: Nvidia’s board is preparing to remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reports, three days after the same board said it trusted his leadership. The move follows Huang’s admission that he had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials believe works for China’s spy services. According to WSJ, Huang also had a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, the senior Nvidia executive who runs the company’s healthcare business.The board was planning to meet as soon as Wednesday to decide his future, WSJ reported. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and built a gaming chip startup into the AI industry’s main chip supplier, with an estimated 90% share of that market. Nvidia shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading on the news.Nvidia board backed Jensen Huang just days before the ouster reportOn November 8, Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. At the time, it said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is running the probe.The same day, Huang admitted the affair in a letter to employees and apologised to his family. “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy,” he wrote.Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Its Malaysian sister company bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia-powered equipment between June 2024 and February 2026. US officials suspect Megaspeed of diverting some of those chips to China. A Commerce Department probe into the firm began in late 2024 and has since moved to the Justice Department, which WSJ says is now leading multiple investigations involving her. China has denied the espionage claims, and Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment.Kimberly Powell relationship puts Nvidia’s own conduct rules in focusPowell, 48, joined Nvidia in 2008 and has headed its healthcare unit since late 2017. People who worked at the company say the relationship was discussed internally. Two of them said the pair were filmed being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia’s GTC conference in March. Huang’s security team then had the bystander who filmed them sign a non-disclosure agreement. Both are married to other people.Nvidia’s code of conduct asks employees to avoid conflicts that arise from personal relationships. Asked about Powell over the phone, Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” and hung up. Powell has not commented.Boards have acted on this before. Intel’s Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a past relationship with an employee, and McDonald’s removed Steve Easterbrook a year later for similar breaches.Nvidia has no succession plan for Jensen HuangThe harder question for the board is who comes next. Huang, 63, has around 60 direct reports and has said he doesn’t believe in succession planning. He is also Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a stake of about 3.56%. The company’s own proxy statement warns that Nvidia is “highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team.” WSJ notes there is no clear successor.Pressure is building outside Nvidia too. Republican leaders of three House committees have asked Huang for a closed-door briefing on his dealings with Alice Huang. A class-action shareholder lawsuit was also filed on Monday in a California federal court.President Donald Trump was briefed on the intelligence about a year ago and took no action. He has stood by Huang, calling him an “amazing guy” and an “honorable man” who did not know she was a suspected spy.On Sunday, the board said it trusted Huang to lead. By Wednesday, it was deciding whether Nvidia, a company he has run for 33 years, can carry on without him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After 27 years flying to remote communities, Australian nurse Karen Barlow is retiring; the Royal Flying Doctor Service veteran says the moments she remembers most are parents holding sick children's hands
articles.summary: We often associate hospitals and treatment with doctors.
articles.body: We often associate hospitals and treatment with doctors. While they are the heroes who help us recover, we sometimes forget the other people who make our experience a little easier. Nurses work day and night, often putting their own needs aside to care for patients, comfort worried families and help with the little things we might otherwise overlook. They are there during some of the most frightening and vulnerable moments of our lives, and their kindness can stay with us long after we leave the hospital.One such unsung hero is Australian nurse Karen Barlow, who is preparing to retire after spending 27 years with the Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS), bringing medical care to people living in some of Australia's most remote communities. While her career has taken her across thousands of kilometres, introduced her to royalty and given her experiences most people can only imagine, she says it is not the grand moments she remembers most. Instead, it is the sight of parents holding their sick children's hands, reassuring them through difficult journeys.A career that took nursing to the skiesFor most nurses, a typical day might involve working in a hospital ward, attending to patients or helping doctors with treatments. But Barlow's workplace was a little different. As a senior flight nurse with the RFDS, she spent nearly 3 decades providing medical assistance to people who could be hundreds of kilometres away from the nearest major hospital.The Royal Flying Doctor Service plays an important role in Australia, particularly for people living in rural and remote areas. When someone needs urgent medical attention and cannot easily reach a hospital, the service brings healthcare to them. Its work includes emergency air retrievals, remote medical clinics and telehealth services, ensuring that distance does not become a barrier to receiving treatment.Barlow was a founding member of the service's Dubbo base in New South Wales. Before joining the aeromedical team, she had already built experience in midwifery, acute care and emergency medicine. Having grown up on the land herself, she understood the realities of life in rural communities and the importance of having medical assistance close at hand.The scale of the service is quite remarkable. The NSW division operates 14 aircraft, covering approximately three million kilometres every year and providing around 90,000 instances of care through its various services. Across Australia, RFDS crews made contact with approximately 345,000 patients in 2023-24, with around 33,000 people flown for treatment. Barlow is one of the nurses who have contributed greatly to this cause.The moments that stay with usWhen someone spends 27 years in a profession, they are bound to have some interesting stories. For Barlow, some of her most unforgettable memories have little to do with medical emergencies or the number of lives she may have helped.One incident involved a little boy who had broken his arm after jumping on a bunk bed with his brothers. He was travelling with his foster father from their remote town to Dubbo for treatment. The family was in the process of adopting him, and during the journey, Barlow noticed something that moved her deeply.The father leaned over and held the little boy's hand throughout the flight. The child, in turn, could not take his eyes off the man sitting beside him. It was a simple moment, but one that said so much about love, trust and the feeling of being safe with someone.For Barlow, watching the two together was beautiful. After all, sometimes the most reassuring thing a frightened child needs is not a complicated explanation or a grand gesture. It is simply knowing that someone they love is right there.Another memory involved a young girl from a rural community who suddenly fell seriously ill. She had always been happy and healthy, but her condition deteriorated so quickly that she had to be placed on life support during a flight to Sydney.Her father struggled to make sense of how quickly everything had changed. He told Barlow that if someone had offered him a million dollars the previous day to bet that he would be in such a situation, he would never have believed it.It is difficult to imagine the fear that comes with watching your child become seriously ill, particularly when you are far from home and being flown somewhere unfamiliar for treatment. For families like these, the flight nurses are not just medical professionals. They are also the people offering reassurance when everything around them feels uncertain.These are the moments Barlow says she will carry with her as she steps away from the profession.A few encounters with royaltyOf course, 27 years in the skies also came with a few rather unexpected experiences. Barlow has met royalty, not once but twice!During a 2012 visit to the Longreach base, she met King Charles and Queen Camilla, who were then the Prince of Wales and Duchess of Cornwall. The medical crew had been waiting inside a hot aircraft before meeting the royal couple and were understandably drenched in sweat by the time they stepped out.Queen Camilla even joked that she understood their discomfort, explaining that the humidity had been so bad that she had nearly needed to call the medical team herself. Barlow's response was that they would certainly have come to her rescue!Six years later, she also met Prince Harry and Meghan Markle when the Duke and Duchess of Sussex visited Dubbo shortly after their wedding. Harry was particularly interested in understanding how the service operated and how it recruited its nurses.While meeting members of the royal family is certainly an unusual career highlight, Barlow's heart seems to belong to the ordinary people she has encountered along the way.A job built on trust and kindnessLeaving a profession after nearly three decades is never easy, especially when it has become such an important part of one's identity. Barlow has described her work as the best job in the world, but she also understands the responsibility that comes with it.Flight nurses often meet people on what could be the worst day of their lives. Some patients have never even been on an aeroplane before, let alone experienced being flown to another city for urgent medical treatment. They are frightened, vulnerable and placing an enormous amount of trust in the people looking after them.For Barlow, being able to reassure them and make them feel better has been one of the most meaningful parts of her work.As she prepares to retire, there will undoubtedly be plenty of people who remember the nurse who helped them through a frightening journey. Perhaps some will remember her medical expertise, while others will remember a comforting conversation or a reassuring smile.But her own memories will remain with those families, too. The father holding his foster son's hand, the little girl fighting for her life and the countless ordinary Australians who came together to support one another.Sometimes, being a hero is as simple as showing up when someone needs you, holding their hand when they are scared and making an unfamiliar journey feel a little less frightening. After 27 years of doing exactly that, Karen Barlow may be leaving the skies, but the kindness she has brought into so many lives will continue to travel much further.You use AI every day. articles.body: Indonesia’s Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned on Thursday after questions over his eligibility for the office intensified following court rulings that disputed his educational qualifications. The 39-year-old, son of former president Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People’s Consultative Assembly (MPR) at the parliament building in Jakarta, setting in motion a process to approve his departure and select a replacement.Raka’s resignation comes after the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements. It was not immediately clear whether the president had accepted his resignation offer at the time.Two sources at the parliamentary upper house had earlier told Reuters that Raka was expected to submit his resignation letter on Thursday morning.What happens nextUnder Indonesian law, the leadership of the People’s Consultative Assembly must establish a special committee to examine whether Raka violated the constitution by serving as vice-president despite allegedly failing to meet the eligibility requirements.If lawmakers find sufficient grounds for the accusation, the House must approach the Constitutional Court for a ruling on whether a constitutional violation took place.The parliamentary process will also oversee the approval of Raka’s resignation and the selection of his replacement.You use AI every day. articles.title: An 1856 steamboat sank near Kansas City; 132 years later, its 200-ton cargo was found 45 feet beneath a cornfield, including tools, weapons and pickles
articles.summary: In a remarkable excavation effort, a team of friends unearthed the sunken steamboat Arabia, lost in 1856, along with its astonishing cargo including tools, weapons, and even preserved pickles, now housed in a Kansas City museum.
articles.body: What would you expect to find under a farmer’s cornfield? Soil, stones, possibly an old tool. A group of family and friends dug up a steamboat from an era even before the American Civil War. The steamboat, Arabia, sank in the Missouri River near Kansas City in 1856, and its cargo remained hidden for 132 years. In a 2004 interview with the National Endowment for the Humanities, brothers David and Greg Hawley described how that team dug it up in 1988, long after the river had shifted away.A tree trunk hidden underwater The Arabia was built in Pennsylvania in 1853, and was only three years old when it went down. It carried both passengers and cargo from St. Louis to 16 different settlements located west of Kansas City. On 5 September 1856, the boat hit a tree hidden under the water. David Hawley explained that the tree punched a hole in the boat, causing it to sink in the mud. Although the passengers were lucky enough to survive, they lost all their cargo. The Arabia Steamboat Museum puts the cargo that was lost at approximately 200 tons. Hidden tree trunks, called snags, were a deadly danger on the Missouri. Greg Hawley estimated that some 400 boats had sunk in the river, and about 70% of those were said to have sunk because of snags. Gradually, the Arabia was covered with sediment and the river slowly changed its course. David Hawley said that this left the wreck on dry land about half a mile from the river and buried 45 feet deep under a cornfield in Kansas.How a few ordinary men found itThe team wasn't a group of trained explorers. They were three refrigeration repairmen, a restaurant owner, and a man who dug sewer ditches. David Hawley used an old newspaper from 1856 which placed the sinking about a mile below the town of Parkville, Missouri. Then he traced an old map onto a modern map to follow the path of a once-flowing river. Finally, he walked the cornrows with a metal detector and found the boilers and engines. Digging the boat out was basically a fight against water. The team lowered the water table with 20 irrigation wells pumping 20,000 gallons a minute, day and night. Greg Hawley recalled that the whole excavation took four and a half months. He said the pace was faster than most archaeologists would like, so the team had to balance speed with careful records. These details come from the brothers’ own account.What was really inside There were rumours that the Arabia carried 400 barrels of bourbon whisky, but what was recovered from the mud was quite different. The first item found was a small rubber shoe marked “Goodyear” with an 1849 patent date. According to David Hawley, the items recovered included Asian silk, English dishes, South American tobacco, and French perfume. Among other things listed by the museum, which keeps the collection, are tools, weapons and clothing, as well as preserved fruits and green sweet pickles, which it says were still edible when they were dug up.The brothers started out as treasure hunters, but that changed when they opened passengers’ luggage. Greg Hawley described the box containing patched trousers, worn boots, two jugs and a small coin purse. From these items, the team pictured a poor traveller who still chose to head west in hopes of a better life. Instead of selling, the brothers decided to keep the cargo together, which now lives in the Arabia Steamboat Museum in Kansas City, Missouri.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Pakistan announces schedule for Guru Nanak’s 557th birth anniversary celebrations despite Attari-Wagah closure
articles.summary: AMRITSAR: Despite the continued closure of the Attari-Wagah international land border following Operation Sindoor, the Pakistan government has announced a
articles.body: AMRITSAR: Despite the continued closure of the Attari-Wagah international land border following Operation Sindoor, the Pakistan government has announced a programme for the 557th birth anniversary celebrations of Guru Nanak Dev, expecting between 2,300 and 2,700 Sikh pilgrims from India for the November 24 event at Nankana Sahib.Pakistan has also maintained that the Kartarpur Corridor remains open from its side, although pilgrim movement through it continues to be suspended by India.According to Pak media reports, the programme was finalised at a meeting of the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (PSGPC), chaired by its president and Punjab provincial minister for minority affairs and human rights, Ramesh Singh Arora, to review arrangements for the celebrations.As per the schedule, Indian Sikh pilgrims are expected to arrive in Pakistan through the Attari international border on November 22. The main ceremony will be held on November 24 at Gurdwara Janam Asthan, Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Nanak Dev. The pilgrims are scheduled to return on December 1.Reacting to Pakistan’s announcement, Sikh scholar Jagdeep Singh said the proposed pilgrimage programme assumes significance amid strained India-Pakistan ties and the continued closure of the Attari-Wagah border after Operation Sindoor. “Keeping the border open would serve the interests of both countries and, above all, make it easier for devotees to visit their historic religious shrines,” said Jagdeep.Interestingly, while Pakistan maintains that the Kartarpur corridor is operational on its side and has expressed readiness to facilitate Sikh devotees, India has suspended pilgrim movement through it since May 2025.In a statement, Arora said Pakistani diplomatic missions had been instructed to facilitate visa issuance for Sikh pilgrims. He also urged India to allow the Sikh sangat to visit its historic shrines.According to reports, the arrangements reviewed at the meeting include air-conditioned buses, accommodation, langar, medical facilities, mineral water and currency exchange services. articles.title: Stewardess Violet Jessop was aboard the RMS Olympic when it collided with a warship in 1911, survived the Titanic sinking in 1912, and then survived the sinking of its sister ship Britannic in 1916
articles.summary: Violet Jessop survived three maritime disasters involving the Olympic-class ships, a record that earned her the nickname “Miss Unsinkable.” According to
articles.body: Violet Jessop survived three maritime disasters involving the Olympic-class ships, a record that earned her the nickname “Miss Unsinkable.” According to Wikipedia, All That’s Interesting and Sky History, she was aboard the RMS Olympic when it collided with HMS Hawke in 1911, escaped the Titanic’s sinking in 1912, and survived the sinking of the HMHS Britannic in 1916.Her story is remarkable not only because she lived through so much, but because she kept returning to sea afterward. Jessop worked as a stewardess and later as a nurse during World War I, and she continued serving on ocean liners long after the disasters that should have been enough to end any maritime career.A difficult early lifeViolet Constance Jessop was born on October 2, 1887, near Bahía Blanca, Argentina, to Irish immigrant parents. She was the eldest of nine children, six of whom survived infancy, and she spent much of her childhood helping care for her younger siblings.As a child, Jessop contracted tuberculosis, an illness doctors predicted would be fatal. She survived, though the experience left a lasting impression on her sense of resilience.When she was 16, her father died after complications from surgery, and the family moved to England. Jessop attended a convent school before leaving to help support the family when her mother became ill.Following in her mother’s footsteps, she applied for work as a stewardess. At 21, she joined the Royal Mail Line aboard the Orinoco in 1908, beginning a career at sea that would become one of the most extraordinary in maritime history.The Olympic collisionIn 1911, Jessop joined the White Star Line and was assigned to the RMS Olympic, the largest civilian liner of its time. The ship was the first of three Olympic-class vessels built in Belfast, alongside the Titanic and the Britannic.On September 20, 1911, the Olympic left Southampton and collided with the British warship HMS Hawke in the Solent. The impact caused significant damage to the Olympic, but no one died and the ship managed to return to port without assistance.The collision was costly for White Star, which had to pay for extensive repairs and lost revenue while the Olympic was out of service. An inquiry also found the company responsible for the incident.Jessop did not mention the collision in her memoirs, but she remained with the Olympic until April 1912, when she was transferred to the Titanic. That move would place her at the center of one of the most famous maritime disasters in history.Surviving the TitanicJessop boarded the Titanic on April 10, 1912, at the age of 24. Four days later, on April 14, the ship struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank about two hours and forty minutes later.In her memoirs, Jessop described being ordered onto deck to serve as an example for non-English-speaking passengers who could not follow the crew’s instructions. She watched as lifeboats were loaded, then was ordered into lifeboat 16.As the boat was lowered, Titanic’s sixth officer, James Paul Moody, handed her a baby to look after. Jessop and the other survivors were rescued the next morning by the RMS Carpathia and taken to New York.According to Jessop, while aboard the Carpathia, a woman, presumably the baby’s mother, grabbed the child from her arms and ran off crying without saying a word. The moment became one of the most haunting details of her account.Nearly 1,500 people died in the Titanic disaster, but Jessop survived. Instead of leaving the sea behind, she returned to work, a decision that would soon place her in danger again.The Britannic disasterDuring World War I, Jessop became a nurse with the Voluntary Aid Detachment and served aboard the HMHS Britannic, the youngest of the Olympic-class ships. The vessel had been converted into a hospital ship and was carrying wounded troops from the Gallipoli campaign.On November 21, 1916, the Britannic struck a German naval mine in the Aegean Sea and sank within 55 minutes. Thirty of the 1,066 people aboard died, but Jessop survived, though not without injury.As the ship listed, lifeboats were pulled toward one of Britannic’s giant spinning propellers, which had lifted partly out of the water. The boats were smashed, and Jessop had to jump into the sea to avoid being pulled under.She suffered a traumatic head injury in the process. Years later, a doctor discovered she had sustained a skull fracture, a detail she only learned long after the event.Jessop later described watching the Britannic go down, saying the ship “dipped her head a little, then a little lower and still lower” before taking a final plunge into the depths. Her words captured the horror of seeing another White Star liner disappear beneath the waves.A life after disasterAfter the war, Jessop returned to work for White Star Line in 1920. She later joined the Red Star Line and then the Royal Mail Line again, completing two around-the-world cruises aboard the Belgenland.At 36, she married John James Lewis, a fellow White Star steward, though the marriage ended in divorce after about a year. She eventually retired to Great Ashfield in Suffolk, where she lived until her death in 1971 at the age of 83.Her story has been retold in books, films and documentaries, including the 1958 film A Night to Remember and James Cameron’s 1997 Titanic. In the 1979 television movie S.O.S. Titanic, Jessop was portrayed by Madge Ryan.Jessop’s life remains a reminder that survival is not always about luck. Sometimes it is about persistence, courage and the willingness to keep moving forward, even when the sea has already taken so much.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A soldier’s 1945 love letter to his future wife vanished inside a record; 70 years later, a Denver woman found it in a thrift-store purchase and returned it to him
articles.summary: A touching story of a WWII veteran who received a long-lost love letter written in 1945, discovered inside a record by a Denver woman at a thrift store, bringing back memories of his late wife.
articles.body: A love letter can slip out of sight and get lost in time. Yet one from 1945 made a very long journey and found its way back to its author. According to the US Department of Veterans Affairs, a woman in Denver found the letter tucked inside a record she had purchased at a thrift store. It was written by Bill Moore, a World War II veteran who was 20 years old at the time. Seventy years later, he read it again and cried.A young soldier writes to the girl he lovesIn January 1945, Bill Moore was a soldier serving in Europe with the Third Army. He had been on furlough when he met his future wife, Bernadean Gibson. Away from her, he sat down to write a letter which begins with the line, “My darling, lovable, alluring Bernadean.” He tells her that he is the luckiest guy in the world and that even her name sounds lovely to him. He also writes that he had never been so homesick for anyone in his life. Years later, Moore reflected on the significance of such words. When you are separated for that reason, wondering whether you will ever see that person again, every chance to communicate felt wonderful, he said.A record, a thrift store, and a stranger Decades went by, and the letter was lost to the family. Bernadean passed away in 2010. Local news coverage reported that Bernadean’s mother had kept the couple's letters for years, but the family could no longer find them. Moore's daughter, Melinda Gale, said this is the only love letter from that time that survived. Then the letter turned up in the most surprising place. Ilene Ortiz bought an old record at a thrift store and found Moore's letter inside it. She thought it was such a romantic letter that somebody should have it. Ortiz reached out to the Denver television station KMGH, or 7NEWS, asking for help in locating the owner. 7NEWS located the family, and the letter found its way to Gale. She explained that the letter meant a lot to her mother, who talked about it often.Tears and memories at 90 Moore was already 90 years old by then, living in an assisted living facility in Aurora, Colorado. The author of the letter wasn't far away after all. As he read his words again, he cried. However, he could also laugh through his tears at his choice of sweet words. “It probably gets worse,” he said. Talking to Lindsay Watts from 7NEWS, he said, “I was really surprised.” He added that he had no idea that the letter would show up in such a way and actually reach him. Moore and Bernadean had been married for 63 years. Speaking of her, Moore said, “I loved her.” His daughter called the letter a wonderful gift, saying it felt amazing to go back to the very beginning after so many years together.Why wartime letters mattered Letters meant a lot to soldiers during World War II. The Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum explains that, to deal with the huge volume of mail being sent to and from service members that was competing with vital supplies for cargo space, the V-mail system was developed. It adds that letter writing was encouraged because it was believed to boost the morale of American soldiers. We don't know if this particular soldier's letter travelled as a V-mail. Moore’s words to the woman he loved and later married found their way back to him, and it all began with a stranger who cared enough to return the letter to its writer.You use AI every day. The board was planning to meet as soon as Wednesday to decide his future, WSJ reported.Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and built a gaming chip startup into the AI industry’s main chip supplier, with an estimated 90% share of that market. articles.title: LaGuardia’s 1934–36 crackdown drove nearly all New York slot machines from the city; a 1937 photo showed confiscated machines, pinball games and guns being taken out to sea
articles.summary: Explore the fascinating history of Mayor LaGuardia's seizure and ocean dumping of slot machines in 1930s New York, highlighting the crackdown on illegal gambling and its long-term impacts.
articles.body: Imagine a tugboat leaving New York filled with guns and slot machines, on its way to dump the lot at sea. It might sound like something straight out of a movie, but it really did happen. David Blankenhorn, in a 2013 report for the Institute for American Values, wrote that Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia ordered police to seize slot machines in January 1934, just days after taking office. His crackdown quickly turned into a very public campaign.A city packed with slot machines A walk around New York in January 1934 would have left you convinced that slot machines were everywhere. Blankenhorn estimated that there were 25,000 to 30,000 slot machines operating openly in the city in that month alone. These machines could be found in small shops, diners, candy stores, and cigar shops across the five boroughs. A single nickel slot machine in the right spot was said to make up to $20 per day. This was a big business. New York City’s slot machines brought in an estimated $57 million in 1932. He adds that the police took no action to stop the activity but actually encouraged it, and any shop owner complaining was likely to see his property damaged.Why LaGuardia called the mechanical pickpocketsLaGuardia was no puritan. The report said he saw casual gambling as relatively harmless and even opposed Prohibition. He was angry that ordinary people were being cheated, and he called the machines “mechanical pickpockets.” He put on a free public exhibit of fifty slot machines at Rockefeller Center. Its theme was “You Can't Win.” Scholars from New York University announced that the machines paid out only about 75.6 cents in prizes for every dollar put in.LaGuardia would not back down. He took over a police station for a day to hear a case of slot machines himself. The city took the fight all the way to the US Supreme Court, but the justices never ruled on the machines themselves. New York passed a new state law that made slot machines a misdemeanor. The Supreme Court said in May 1934 the new law changed the situation, overturned the appeals court ruling and sent it back to be dismissed.Smashed, sunk, and dumpedOctober 1934 stands out particularly. The report states that the mayor, his police and fire commissioners, and a group of labourers loaded 1,155 machines confiscated by the city government onto a barge at Pier A. They set sail for Long Island Sound, where LaGuardia used a sledgehammer to destroy several of these machines. These destroyed machines were then sunk into the Sound. In 1936, another 1,300 machines were smashed and thrown overboard into the Sound.The dumping didn't stop there. The Brooklyn Public Library’s digital collection holds a photograph dated 1937. The picture's caption describes the tug Manhattan, loaded with slot machines, pinball games and guns of all sorts, leaving Pier 4 at the Battery to dump police seized goods into the ocean. The caption says ocean and doesn't name the mayor either. This hints at a trip separate from the earlier dumps.Did the crackdown work According to the report, it largely did. LaGuardia drove nearly all slot machine operators out of the city. Soon after the 1936 dump, nearly all the machines were gone. Blankenhorn also notes that by 2013, the computerised slot machines had come to drive the casino industry, and he uses LaGuardia’s story to argue against state-backed casinos. However, not everyone shares the same view and gambling policy remains a matter of debate even today.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Mumbai man pays Livspace Rs 71.62 lakh for premium flat interiors, finds inferior materials and exposed live wires, wife suffers head injury after heavy kitchen shutter falls on her; consumer commission orders firm to pay nearly Rs 87.16 lakh
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has held interior design firm Livspace India Pvt Ltd guilty of deficiency in service
articles.body: MUMBAI: The Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has held interior design firm Livspace India Pvt Ltd guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices over a Goregaon flat renovation that left exposed live wires and saw a heavy kitchen shutter fall on a woman's head.The commission expressed grave concern over the company's alleged negligence and hazardous workmanship, observing that it had promised premium materials and branded products, including its “Regalia” modular kitchen range, but systematically substituted them with inferior alternatives.“This bait-and-switch tactic constitutes an unfair trade practice, as it misleads consumers regarding the standard, quality, and grade of services and goods promised,” the commission said.It directed Livspace to pay complainant Deepak Ruiya nearly Rs 87.16 lakh, comprising a refund of Rs 71.62 lakh and Rs 15.54 lakh in interest and compensation. The commission also found that the company had failed to complete the renovation within the agreed timeline, used inferior materials and left the premises in an unsafe condition.“The record evidences severe safety breaches, including uninsulated live electrical wires left exposed behind bed panels, posing a life-threatening hazard to the complainant’s children and elderly family members. Furthermore, the installation was so shoddy that a heavy kitchen shutter collapsed directly onto the complainant’s wife's head,” it said.The commission also flagged the company's administrative chaos and lack of professional oversight. It noted that senior designers and project personnel exited without notice, while Livspace changed project managers and designers without Ruiya's consent, leaving the project without proper supervision for months.“This erratic management directly contributed to substandard execution and severe delay,” the commission observed.Ruiya filed the complaint in 2025 against Livspace India Pvt Ltd, formerly known as Home Interior Designs E-Commerce Pvt Ltd. He had hired the company to design and renovate his flat at Kalpataru Radiance in Goregaon West for Rs 71.62 lakh.Livspace had assured him that the work would be completed within 90 to 120 days. The original handover deadline was July 1, 2024, which was later extended to September 1, 2024.According to Ruiya, despite substantial payments, the project remained incomplete, with designers and managers being changed without notice. He also alleged that the company used lower-grade materials instead of those promised, including HDHMR instead of the specified grade of plywood and “Infiniti” shutters instead of the “Regalia” range.The complaint also highlighted serious safety lapses. Ruiya alleged that live electrical wires were left uninsulated behind bed panels and that, on January 2, 2025, a heavy kitchen shutter fell on his wife’s head due to faulty installation.After issuing a legal notice on December 5, 2024, he approached the commission seeking a refund, compensation and litigation costs.Livspace failed to appear before the commission despite being served notice and a newspaper publication. The matter consequently proceeded ex parte in July 2025.The commission noted that Ruiya's affidavit, payment records, emails, photographs and survey material remained unrebutted. It held that the company's failure to meet even the extended deadline and its substitution of promised materials with inferior alternatives amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.Apart from refunding the amount paid with interest, Livspace was directed to pay compensation for mental agony, harassment and the safety risks caused, along with litigation costs.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Rejected by his mother, bullied by older monkeys and raised with a stuffed toy, Punch is now showing a softer side of care towards a younger macaque
articles.summary: It is not often that the internet collectively roots for anything.
articles.body: It is not often that the internet collectively roots for anything. But Punch, the Japanese macaque whose early life was marked by rejection, loneliness and a stuffed orangutan he rarely let go of, managed to do just that. The tiny monkey who once seemed to find safety only in the arms of a toy is growing up, and his latest appearance at Ichikawa City Zoo and Botanical Gardens in Japan has offered fans a heartwarming glimpse of a new chapter. Punch has been spotted taking an interest in a younger baby macaque, a moment that has drawn attention because of how far he has come since his own difficult beginning, according to a report by PEOPLE.For those who followed his story from the beginning, the sight carries a special significance. Not long ago, Punch was the one who needed comfort. Now, as he becomes more familiar with the other members of his troop, he is being seen approaching a much younger monkey. The footage does not establish that he has taken on a parental role, but it offers a tender contrast to the images that first made him famous: a tiny macaque dragging a toy almost as big as himself, seemingly looking for the security he could not find with his mother.In a recent update on X, the zoo shared footage of Punch, giving fans another glimpse of the monkey who has become one of its most recognisable residents. The post was also a reminder that his progress has not happened on its own. Behind the viral videos and the affection of millions of strangers are the keepers who have watched over him, adjusted his care and helped him gradually become comfortable around other macaques.“Punch and the other animals’ conditions change from day to day,” the zoo wrote in the post, translated from Japanese. “We observe them, interact with them, and provide care.”The zoo added that keepers adjust the animals’ feeding routines according to the season and weather, crediting their daily attention for Punch’s continued health. It also asked supporters to recognise the staff whose work has helped him thrive.Born in July 2025, Punch was unable to receive care from his mother shortly after birth. He was taken in by zookeepers, who hand-raised him and bottle-fed him. For a baby Japanese macaque, being able to cling to its mother is important not only for comfort but also for developing the strength and instincts needed to navigate life. Without that contact, Punch needed an alternative.The keepers tried different substitutes, including towels and other soft toys, before settling on an orange stuffed orangutan from IKEA. The toy became his constant companion. He would drag it around his enclosure, hug it and return to it after difficult interactions with other monkeys. Pictures and videos of the tiny macaque clutching the oversized plushie spread rapidly online, turning him into an unlikely global sensation and inspiring the hashtag #HangInTherePunch.His journey into the troop was not always easy. Videos showed older macaques chasing him away or scolding him, prompting concern among viewers who feared he was being bullied. The zoo later explained that such interactions could be part of the troop's social hierarchy and that the behaviour should not automatically be interpreted as bullying. Keepers continued monitoring his interactions as he learned to live alongside the other monkeys.Slowly, the images began to change. Punch was seen spending more time with other macaques, playing, receiving attention and becoming less dependent on his stuffed companion. His first birthday in July brought another reminder of how many people had followed his journey: fans sent more than 2,500 birthday cards to the zoo.Now, the sight of Punch showing interest in a younger macaque has given that journey another emotional turn. The baby who once needed a substitute companion is no longer alone in the same way. He is still young and learning to navigate life in the troop, but he is increasingly participating in the world around him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ariana Grande's former London penthouse is on sale for £16.95 million; singer stayed in the luxury residence while filming Wicked
articles.summary: Ariana Grande's former London residence, where the singer stayed while filming the Wicked movies, has returned to the property market with an asking price
articles.body: Ariana Grande's former London residence, where the singer stayed while filming the Wicked movies, has returned to the property market with an asking price of £16.95 million. Located in the exclusive Buxmead development on The Bishops Avenue in Hampstead, north London, the penthouse combines expansive living spaces, private leisure facilities and extensive security. The property, which Grande rented during her time working in Britain, offers a glimpse into the accommodation chosen by international celebrities seeking privacy while remaining close to film studios and the city's amenities.Ariana Grande's former London penthouse is on sale for £16.95 millionAccording to Mansion Global, the penthouse is being marketed for £16.95 million, equivalent to approximately $22.8 million at the time of its report. It sits within Buxmead, a residential development comprising 20 apartments on The Bishops Avenue, a street widely known as Billionaires' Row because of its concentration of expensive homes and wealthy residents.The property became associated with Grande during her stay in London for the filming of Wicked and its sequel. The development's location near Elstree Studios, where much of the production took place, made it a practical choice for the singer and actress.The National reported in May 2026 that Grande had rented the apartment while working on the films. Its proximity to the studios, combined with the development's security arrangements, offered a setting suited to a high-profile resident who needed both convenience and discretion.What does the 9,677-square-foot residence offer insideThe scale of the apartment is among its defining features. UK Sotheby's International Realty, which is marketing the property alongside Alexander Main, describes the penthouse as occupying the entire third floor of Buxmead.According to the agency's report, the residence covers 9,677 square feet and includes 5 bedrooms and 6 bathrooms. Its main reception room stretches 44 feet, with full-height windows providing views towards Kenwood Park. The layout also includes a formal dining room and a dedicated bar, making it suitable for both everyday living and entertaining.The principal bedroom suite has 2 dressing rooms, a spacious bathroom and direct access to the terrace. 4 additional bedrooms are arranged in a separate wing, offering further space for family members or guests.The property was completed through a three-year interior fit-out after Dean Main, founder of investment company Henigman, acquired 11 apartments at Buxmead in 2019. Mansion Global reported that the penthouse had originally been purchased in shell-and-core condition, with SHH Architecture & Interior Design responsible for its interiors.How does the penthouse combine luxury with private leisure facilitiesA separate lower floor and extensive shared amenities. Beyond its main living areas, the apartment has a lower level designed around entertainment, relaxation and practical facilities. UK Sotheby's International Realty reports that a private lift connects the principal floor to this additional space, which contains a cinema, games room, gym, study and secondary kitchen.Mansion Global also describes a wet bar and a separate dining room on the lower level. The bedrooms and study open onto a patio, extending the private living areas beyond the interior.One of the more unusual features is the underground six-car garage, which can be reached directly through the apartment's private lift. The arrangement allows residents to move between their vehicles and living spaces without passing through shared areas.The development itself adds another layer of amenities. The National reports that Buxmead has an indoor swimming pool, cinema, games room and treatment areas. UK Sotheby's International Realty also lists a 25-metre pool, fitness centre, spa, sauna, steam room, hammam and Jacuzzi, alongside an 18-seat cinema and concierge services.Buxmead appeals to celebrities seeking privacySecurity is a central part of the property's appeal. Buxmead is set within 2.5 acres of landscaped gardens on The Bishops Avenue, with a uniformed security team and arrangements designed to limit unwanted attention.Becky Fatemi, executive partner at UK Sotheby's International Realty, described the development as London's residential Fort Knox in comments reported by Mansion Global. The development was designed by Harrison Varma with security-conscious clients in mind. Its private gardens and controlled access offer an additional degree of separation from the surrounding neighbourhood.For Grande, the location also had a practical advantage. articles.title: This American town has a single resident and she is the Mayor, bartender and an entire government
articles.summary: Who do you think keeps the lights on around here? Being a mayor in Monowi, Nebraska, is a tough job.
articles.body: Who do you think keeps the lights on around here?Being a mayor in Monowi, Nebraska, is a tough job. You have to run the administration, manage the finances, keep the library open and, perhaps most importantly, make sure nobody's glass stays empty for too long. But what happens when you are the only person living in the town you govern?Elsie Eiler is the sole resident of Monowi and the woman keeping the entire town alive. Recognised by Guinness World Records as the incorporated town with the world's lowest population, Monowi is quite literally a one-woman show. And while the title might sound like the beginning of a lonely story, Elsie's life is anything but a tale of someone waiting to be rescued.Monowi was not always this quiet. Like many small American towns, it began as a railway settlement in the early 1900s. The railway brought people, businesses and opportunities, and the village eventually grew into a thriving little community. At its peak in 1930, it had 123 residents. There were shops, restaurants, a school, a post office and even a church. But as the years passed, younger generations moved away in search of jobs and better opportunities elsewhere. Businesses shut down, the railway disappeared and the population steadily declined. By 1980, only 18 people remained.By 2000, the town had just two residents, Elsie and her husband, Rudy Eiler. A world where it seems its just me and my partner sounds like a dream come true, right? The two had known each other since childhood, having met at the local one-room schoolhouse. They eventually married and settled in Monowi, where they built their lives together. They also purchased the local tavern in 1971, turning it into a familiar meeting place for people in the surrounding area.Unfortunately, when Rudy passed away in 2004, Elsie was left as the town's only inhabitant. While many might have considered moving somewhere with more people around, she decided to stay. This was her home, after all.And she wasn't about to let her husband's memory disappear either. Rudy was an avid reader who had accumulated around 5,000 books over the years. In 2005, Elsie established Rudy's Library in his memory, using his personal collection to create a little public library in the village. Today, it remains one of the three active buildings in Monowi, alongside her home and the tavern. The library operates on an honour system, allowing visitors to browse and borrow books without the usual fuss of library cards and administrative formalities.Running a town of one also comes with its fair share of paperwork. As mayor, Elsie handles the municipal administration, prepares the town's road plans, manages its finances and applies for the funding needed to maintain basic services. She also serves as the town clerk, secretary and treasurer. And then there is her other rather interesting responsibility: issuing herself the annual liquor licence for the tavern she owns and operates. The application goes through the village secretary, who happens to be Elsie. She signs it as the clerk and receives it as the business owner. Getting things done without having to chase anyone for an approval is a dream job; she truly is her own boss!But her administrative duties are only part of her day. At 93, Elsie continues to work at the Monowi Tavern for around 12 hours a day, six days a week. She serves coffee, cooks burgers, pours drinks and welcomes anyone who happens to walk through the door. Her customers include local farmers, regulars from neighbouring towns and curious travellers who have made the journey just to meet the woman behind the town's unusual record.In fact, visitors have arrived from all 50 US states and more than 60 countries. The tavern has become something of a tourist attraction, with people eager to see the famous village sign announcing its population of one. Yet Elsie doesn't seem particularly impressed by her international popularity. She has always been more interested in the people who actually come through the door than the headlines written about her.In Monowi, a neighbour isn't 4 feet apart, but 40 miles away, as she once explained to Country Living. You know how they say, good fences make good neighbours. But, that doesn’t mean the relationship is distant. Instead it is more cordial than ever. Everyone looks out for one another. When it snows, a local farmer might turn up to clear her parking lot and the main street. When the tavern gets busy, friends and acquaintances are happy to lend a hand.During winter, regulars gather at the tavern on Sunday evenings to play euchre, a card game, and spend time catching up. Some customers have known Elsie for decades. Others are younger generations of families who have been visiting the establishment for years. It is a place where people share meals, stories and a little company after a long day. As Matthew 22:39 says, you shall love your neighbor as yourself.This is not a rescue call, not a 'One Less Lonely Girl' storyline waiting to happen. Elsie doesn't need rescuing, and being the only person living in a town doesn't necessarily mean being alone in the world. She has family, friends, familiar faces and a community that continues to show up for her. Her daughter, Rene Lassise, has pointed out that outsiders often miss the camaraderie and genuine connections that keep her mother attached to the place. The town might have only one official resident, but it certainly has more than one person who considers it home.Of course, even Elsie knows that Monowi's future is uncertain. With nobody else living there to take over the administrative responsibilities or keep its businesses running, the town's existence is closely tied to her own. She has admitted that thinking about a time when she might no longer be able to stay makes her sad. She would like to see Monowi continue to exist rather than become another collection of abandoned buildings along a roadside.It is a rather unusual situation. Most people spend their lives looking for somewhere to belong, while Elsie has spent hers holding on to a place that the rest of the world slowly moved away from. Perhaps a town isn't always defined by how many people live in it, how many shops line its streets or how busy its roads are. Sometimes, it is defined by the people who keep showing up, the stories they share and the connections they refuse to let go of.So, who keeps the lights on around here? Well, the mayor does. And she might just be serving you a burger while she is at it. And maybe, this town ain't big enough for two.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Billionaire Nicky Oppenheimer’s family transformed 43 former cattle and sheep farms into a 118,000-hectare wildlife reserve in South Africa’s Kalahari
articles.summary: Billionaire Nicky Oppenheimer's family has helped transform 43 former cattle and sheep farms in South Africa into the 118,000-hectare Tswalu Kalahari
articles.body: Billionaire Nicky Oppenheimer's family has helped transform 43 former cattle and sheep farms in South Africa into the 118,000-hectare Tswalu Kalahari Reserve, one of the country's largest privately protected wilderness areas. The conservation project began under businessman Stephen Boler, who acquired the land in 1995 and started restoring its degraded landscape. After Boler died in 1999, the Oppenheimer family took over the property and continued his vision of returning the land to its natural state. Today, the reserve supports diverse Kalahari wildlife, protects biodiversity and uses sustainable tourism to help fund its long-term conservation efforts.How did Nicky Oppenheimer's family transform 43 farms into a wildlife reserveThe land that now forms Tswalu Kalahari Reserve was originally developed by consolidating cattle farms, with commercial farming attempts dating back to the 19th century. In 1995, Englishman Stephen Boler acquired the collection of farms and named the property Tswalu. Over the following two years, he added 28 more farms and began restoring the landscape.According to Tswalu's Celebrating Tswalu's Living Heritage, Boler's work included dismantling derelict buildings, removing fences and other unwanted infrastructure, and introducing indigenous Kalahari wildlife. His efforts also included the reintroduction of species such as the black rhino and black-maned lion. The reserve's account describes the landscape before restoration as having been affected by cattle farming and neglect.How did Nicky Oppenheimer's family acquire 43 former farms in South AfricaA meeting between Boler and billionaire businessman Nicky Oppenheimer in 1999 played a significant role in determining the property's future. Oppenheimer visited Tswalu at Boler's invitation and recalled being captivated by the Kalahari landscape and its vast open spaces. According to the reserve, Boler had already made considerable progress in transforming the property before their meeting.When Boler died in 1999, his will requested that the property be offered in its entirety to the Oppenheimer family, with the hope that they would continue the conservation work he had started. Nicky Oppenheimer accepted the responsibility and continued the project. The reserve states that the family's subsequent land acquisitions brought the property to a total of 43 former cattle and sheep farms. Reflecting on the continuing commitment, Oppenheimer said: "The work of conservation here will never stop."How large is Tswalu Kalahari Reserve and what wildlife does it protectTswalu Kalahari Reserve covers 118,000 hectares (292,000 acres) of private wilderness in the southern Kalahari. According to its official visitor information, it is the largest private game reserve in South Africa. The reserve provides habitat for several wildlife species, including black-maned lions, desert black rhinos, African wild dogs, white rhinos and cheetahs.The property's conservation importance received formal recognition in 2014, when Tswalu was designated as a protected area. The reserve states that it has since become an important contributor to species conservation and a reservoir of genetic diversity. Research is also a central part of its conservation programme, with projects conducted under the Tswalu Foundation focusing on understanding endangered species and informing the ecological management of the reserve.How does ecotourism support conservation at Tswalu Kalahari ReserveAlongside its conservation activities, Tswalu operates as a low-impact, high-value ecotourism destination. Its official information explains that income from guest stays helps offset the costs of managing the privately protected area. Visitors receive access to the reserve through privately guided safari experiences, with a dedicated vehicle, guide and tracker for each booking.The reserve operates three safari camps: Loapi, The Motse and Tarkuni. Its visitor programme includes game drives, nature walks, rock art walks, animal tracking, birdwatching and opportunities to encounter habituated meerkats. Guests can also learn about research carried out through the Tswalu Foundation. According to the reserve, choosing to stay at Tswalu allows visitors to contribute towards its conservation work, which aims to protect the Kalahari ecosystem and address biodiversity loss.You use AI every day. articles.title: Firecracker dealers push for relaxed Diwali timings from 8 pm to midnight
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Amid widespread criticism over noise violations during Diwali-Kali Puja, which many residents described as among the worst in recent years,
articles.body: KOLKATA: Amid widespread criticism over noise violations during Diwali-Kali Puja, which many residents described as among the worst in recent years, Burrabazar Fireworks Dealers Association president Santanu Dutta defended the use of display fireworks, arguing that fireworks will naturally produce sound and that products sold through licensed channels remain within the Supreme Court’s 125 dB limit.“Anything creating noise will sound loud. Everything is under 125 decibels,” Dutta said. “It appears to be piercing your ears because you don’t hear it all the time. That is why it hurts.”On complaints that crackers were burst well beyond the two-hour window fixed by the Supreme Court, Dutta said the restriction was impractical and should be relaxed. He said he would appeal to the national fireworks federation to move the Supreme Court seeking an extension of the permitted window from two hours to four hours.“Diwali night, people enjoy till midnight. It should be relaxed from 8 pm to 12 midnight. We will appeal to the federation. It will be practical and feasible,” he said.Dutta, who said he works out of Bazi Bazaar and coordinates with the administration, argued that tighter bans often lead to more violations rather than better compliance. “More the bans, the higher the violation. If it is easily available, the craze will go away,” he said.He said that even if firecrackers disturb a section of residents, the celebrations are limited to a one or two festive days. “Around 30% do get disturbed. But this is just one or two days. This is just once in a year,” he reasoned.Dutta also pointed to other occasions when fireworks are used, including Chhath, when crackers are often burst in the early morning. He said that many people stock fireworks in advance and also purchase them from markets outside Burrabazar, including Nungi and Champahati.On the kind of fireworks being sold, Dutta said the demand is now largely for aerial display items, sky shots and repeaters. “Maximum is sky items, sky display, repeater shots,” he said, adding that a three-piece shell costs around Rs 700.He said some traditional crackers such as kali patka have been allowed, while items like chocolate bombs and dodoma remain banned because they are unsafe. “Chocolate bomb, dodoma is banned because it is unsafe,” he said.Dutta said the impact of fireworks varies across localities. In densely populated areas and slums, ground-level noise is more noticeable, while in high-end areas the sound comes both from the lifting charge and from the burst at a height of 100 ft or 200 ft.He said fireworks have long been part of festive culture and questioned why similar discussions do not take place around other celebrations. “Holi, Diwali, Eid, Christmas — this is not discussed. This has been a tradition since childhood. articles.title: Jaden Smith opened a restaurant where money does not decide who eats. No fixed prices, nobody turned away, and people pay what they can to help others eat.
articles.summary: What happens when humanity becomes bigger than money?
articles.body: What happens when humanity becomes bigger than money? In today's world, where it seems that all we hear about is someone getting killed, brothers betraying each other, animals being poached and trees being cut down, stories of kindness almost feel like a rarity. We have become so accustomed to hearing about everything that is going wrong around us that we sometimes forget that there are still people trying to make things right. And sometimes, all it takes is one person's idea to remind us what humanity is supposed to look like.Who doesn't know Jaden Smith, the famous American rapper known for his childhood film roles, music career and unconventional style? But how many people have heard about his acts of kindness? Beyond the fame, music and fashion, Smith has been working on an initiative that challenges one of society’s most persistent problems: hunger. In a world where even a basic meal can be a luxury for many, he came up with an idea that puts human dignity before the ability to pay.“I Love You” more than just wordsJaden came up with an incredible idea of turning three words into something people could actually experience. In July 2019, he launched the I Love You food truck in Los Angeles, bringing free, healthy meals to people experiencing homelessness. The idea was simple but meaningful: nobody should have to worry about whether they can afford their next meal.In a video posted on TikTok on Saturday, Feb. 14, Smith shared his dreams of leveraging his I Love You brand to achieve his goal."Honestly, my dream in life is to have a building on Skid Row where I can give out free meals every single day: breakfast, lunch, dinner,” Smith said. “I can do things inside of it. I can create jobs and a good vibe. That’s my dream. That’s my long-term goal."What started as a food truck was more than just an attempt to distribute free food. It was an effort to make people feel seen, valued and cared for, especially those who are often overlooked by society. For Jaden, saying "I love you" was not enough. He wanted to put those words into action.But Jaden did not want the initiative to remain limited to handing out free meals. He wanted to create a system that could sustain itself and reach more people. The idea was to bring together people who could afford to pay for their meals and those who could not. Someone paying a little extra could help cover the cost of another person's food, creating a chain of kindness where one person's privilege could become another person's support.A different way of looking at the food businessThe food industry is driven by yet a simple idea: you pay for what you eat. But Jaden wanted to challenge this conventional way of looking at a restaurant. His idea was to create a system where the ability to pay would not determine whether someone got to enjoy their meal or not.The concept revolved around a pay-it-forward model. Customers who could afford their food would contribute towards meals for people who could not. In this way, one person’s meal could help provide another person’s meal as well. Rather than making free food entirely dependent on charity, the idea was to build a community-supported system where generosity could keep the initiative going.Netizens loved the shift in perspective. Instead of asking how much profit a restaurant could make from every customer, the initiative raised another question: how many people could it feed? After all, food is one of our most basic needs, and access to it should not depend entirely on how much money someone has in their pocket.Beyond a meal: Building a community around kindnessFor Jaden, this was never just about giving away food. He wanted to do something for people who are often ignored or judged because of their circumstances. Homelessness is not simply about not having a roof over one's head. It also means struggling with everyday things that most of us rarely think twice about, including getting a decent meal.Jaden has also spoken about his dream of building a permanent space on Skid Row where people could get free breakfast, lunch and dinner. He wants the place to offer more than food, with opportunities for people to work and become part of the community. While the idea is still taking shape, it shows that he is thinking beyond occasional food distribution and looking at ways to make the initiative last.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Meet Jhon Jairo 'Popeye' Velásquez, Pablo Escobar's hitman who helped coordinate 3,000 killings before becoming a famous Colombian YouTuber recounting his days in the Medellín cartel
articles.summary: He helped coordinate 3,000 murders, served 23 years in prison and came back only to become one of Colombia's most famous YouTubers.
articles.body: He helped coordinate 3,000 murders, served 23 years in prison and came back only to become one of Colombia's most famous YouTubers. Jhon Jairo Velásquez was one of Pablo Escobar's deadliest hitmen. Nicknamed 'Popeye' his victims included prominent politicians, underworld rivals and even an airplane full of innocent civilians.During the 1980s and early 90s, Velásquez murdered more than 250 people and arranged 3,000 additional killings for Escobar and the Medellín Cartel. He was arrested in 1992 and spent nearly 23 years behind bars for murder, drug trafficking and terrorism, among other crimes. After his release in 2014, he began a career completely unexpected for a criminal, he became a YouTube star. He began a channel titled 'Repentant Popeye' and criticised the Colombian government while recounting some of his most infamous hits, according to a report by All That's Interesting.The boy who dreamed of joining the policeJhon Jairo Velásquez was born in Yarumal, Colombia in 1962. He dropped out of high school to join the Colombian Navy, where he earned the nickname “Popeye” due to his appearance. However, he soon left and started training to become a police officer.When it didn't work out, a friend found 17-year-old Velasquez a job as a driver and bodyguard for a young woman, who also happened to be Pablo Escobar's girlfriend. By the time he was 18, Velásquez had received orders to carry out his first hit for the up-and-coming Medellín Cartel.“I had to kill a bus dispatcher,” Velásquez told Revista Bocas in a 2013 interview. “Back when the man was a driver, the mother of a friend of Pablo Escobar boarded his bus; he pulled away before she could get off, causing her to fall. He left her lying on the ground without offering any help, and she died.”When Escobar's friend asked him to seek revenge, Velásquez was assigned the task. “I handled reconnaissance, tracked the guy down, and killed him,” Velásquez recalled. “I didn’t feel a thing… I haven’t lost any sleep over the acts I’ve committed.”With his first kill under the belt, Velásquez soon gained the trust of Escobar and quickly rose through the ranks of the cartel.The life of a killerOver the next decade, he killed more than 250 people for Escobar. He took out journalists, drug trafficking rivals, high-profile political figures, and even his own girlfriend. Around 1984, Velásquez arranged the murder of Wendy Chavarriaga Gil, who had previously dated Escobar himself. Velásquez loved her, but Escobar believed she was working as an informant, so she had to die. “What happened with Wendy was madness,” Velásquez told Revista Bocas. “I sent a group of guys… who were under my command. I couldn’t bring myself to carry it out personally. I set up a meeting for her, and they took care of it.”In the 1980s, Velásquez was involved in Escobar's most notorious crimes. In January 1988, Velásquez helped orchestrate the kidnapping of Andrés Pastrana Arango, who was running for mayor of Bogotá. The police found him a week later, and he went on to become the president of Colombia in 1998. Just a week after Pastrana’s abduction, the cartel kidnapped Carlos Mauro Hoyos, another Colombian politician. There are several versions of the story, but according to Velásquez himself, he was ordered to assassinate Hoyos. While the Colombian Army was out searching for Hoyos, Velásquez reportedly disguised himself in a sweater and glasses and bypassed a military checkpoint by claiming to be a student delivering medicine to a relative. When he arrived at the ranch where Hoyos was being held, Velásquez shot him three times.The following year, he helped arrange the murder of presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galán, who was shot to death in front of 10,000 people while surrounded by 18 bodyguards as he walked onto a stage in Soacha to give a speech.However, his most famous crime came in November 1989, when he was involved in planning the bombing of Avianca Flight 203. The airplane left Bogotá with 101 passengers and six crew members — and an explosive planted inside. As the plane flew over Soacha, a young man pushed a button that he reportedly thought would record a conversation. Instead, it detonated the bomb, killing all 107 people on board and three more victims on the ground.Escobar targeted the plane because he thought that presidential candidate César Gaviria would be on the flight, but he was not, and he went on to win the 1990 election. By 1991, Escobar had arranged a deal to surrender to Colombian authorities if he could serve his sentence at La Catedral, the luxury prison he built for himself. Velásquez decided to go with him to serve as his bodyguard. And when Escobar eventually escaped and went on the run, Velásquez accompanied him.Finally, in October 1992, Jhon Jairo Velásquez turned himself in as the Medellín Cartel began to crumble. He was convicted of murder, terrorism, extortion, and drug trafficking, and he received the maximum sentence of 30 years. Velásquez was released in 2014, and began an unexpected new career as a YouTuber.A repentant man?Pablo Escobar died in a shootout with the police while Velásquez was behind bars, and Velásquez had decided not to return to his former life of crime. “I want to enjoy the little things in life now. One thing is certain: I will never again accept a contract to kill someone,” he told Revista Bocas a year before his release.Instead, Velásquez started a YouTube channel called “Repentant Popeye,” which gained more than 1.2 million followers. In his videos, he criticised Colombia’s government and recalled several of the murders he committed.Velásquez also helped produce a movie about his life and wrote two books: My Life as a Hitman for Pablo Escobar and Surviving Pablo Escobar: “Popeye” the Hitman.“I’m a professional killer; I killed for money,” Velásquez said in the 2017 documentary Escobar’s Hitman. “I also killed out of love and respect for Pablo Escobar.”As Velásquez told interviewers in 2013, “If Pablo Escobar were to be reborn, I would go with him without thinking.”Then, in 2018, Velásquez returned to prison for extortion and criminal conspiracy. Two years later, on Feb. 6, 2020, he died from oesophageal cancer at age 57.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Anti-India’ campaign: Chinese vloggers in Dhaka scale back activities amid increased surveillance
articles.summary: Chinese vloggers accused of defaming India by filming poor neighbourhoods in Dhaka and falsely portraying the footage as scenes from New Delhi have
articles.body: Chinese vloggers accused of defaming India by filming poor neighbourhoods in Dhaka and falsely portraying the footage as scenes from New Delhi have "scaled down" their activities following increased surveillance by local law enforcement agencies, a Bangladeshi police official said.The authorities stepped up monitoring of the Chinese nationals, around 150 in number, after India expressed concern over the alleged use of Bangladeshi territory to tarnish its image.Also Read | 'This is New Delhi': Chinese vloggers pass off Bangladesh slums as India in bizarre videosAccording to Mohammad Khalid Mansur, officer-in-charge of Dhaka’s Uttara West Police Station, intelligence agencies intensified surveillance of the Chinese nationals and began monitoring them closely. This led to a decline in their activities, the newspaper Prothom Alo reported on Thursday.Earlier, Bangladeshi media reports said the Chinese vloggers were active in Dhaka’s Tekpara and Uttara neighbourhoods, livestreaming footage of narrow streets and impoverished localities on Chinese social media platforms. They are accused of misrepresenting these areas as parts of New Delhi and making "disparaging" comments about the residents’ living conditions.The vloggers filmed people’s homes and everyday activities, at times entering residential premises without permission. Residents were unaware of where the footage was being uploaded or how they were being portrayed.The activities are suspected to be part of a coordinated disinformation campaign.“There was no police surveillance of their activities. More than 100 vloggers were making such videos every day. They also paid Bangladeshi citizens to assist them in this work,” Prothom Alo reported.On Tuesday, the ministry of external affairs in New Delhi called for appropriate action against the vloggers for peddling "false narratives" to defame India.Also Read | 'Unfortunate': Govt condemns anti-India campaign by Chinese vloggers, urges Bangladesh to take actionFollowing the controversy, the Chinese nationals were asked to produce their passports and visas and explain why they were engaging in such activities while visiting Bangladesh on tourist visas.Police also instructed them to leave the country upon the expiry of their authorised stay.However, it remains unclear whether a formal investigation has been initiated into their activities or whether any action has been taken over possible violations of visa conditions.Residents, meanwhile, reported that they had not seen any Chinese nationals in Uttara or Tekpara over the past few days."I have been at home for two days due to illness and have not seen any Chinese citizens around," Md Selim, a Tekpara resident, told the newspaper.Rickshaw puller Imamul Islam described a bridge over a canal near Sector 12 in Uttara as a "hideout" for the Chinese vloggers."They would film us throughout the day and night, including our passengers. I haven't seen them around for some time now," he added.(With PTI inputs)You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
