articles.title: In 2022, Puerto Rico put baseball legend Roberto Clemente's image on license plates without his sons' permission; after they sought $45 million in damages, the US Supreme Court declined their appeal
articles.summary: The U.S.
articles.body: The U.S. Supreme Court has declined to hear the appeal of Roberto Clemente’s sons, ending their effort to challenge Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image on commemorative license plates. According to Reuters, USA Today and NewsNation, the justices rejected the case on November 9 without explanation, leaving in place lower-court rulings that favored Puerto Rico.The dispute began in 2022, when Puerto Rico issued special license plates and vehicle registration tags honoring Clemente on the 50th anniversary of his death. His sons said the territory used their father’s likeness without permission and sought $45 million in damages, along with $3.15 million for alleged trademark infringement. Read more details about this incident, as per the reports, here:A tribute without permissionPuerto Rico’s commemorative plates featured Clemente’s image, his No. 21 and a reference to his 3,000 career hits. The program was intended to mark 50 years since his death and celebrate one of Puerto Rico’s most beloved sports figures. But Clemente’s sons, Roberto Clemente Jr., Luis Roberto Clemente and Roberto Enrique Clemente, said they were never consulted. They argued that the territory appropriated a valuable family asset by using their father’s image without authorization.The license-plate program charged fees of $21 and $5, which raised a combined $15 million for Puerto Rico. The Clemente family said those revenues should have benefited their businesses, which they said protect the Roberto Clemente trademark, safeguard his legacy and promote his philanthropy.The family also objected to the timing. They argued that the fees were collected during a difficult economic period for Puerto Rico, while the island was recovering from bankruptcy, making the decision to charge residents for plates bearing Clemente’s image especially troubling.The legal argumentThe sons filed suit in federal court in Puerto Rico, claiming that the government’s use of the trademark violated the Fifth Amendment’s prohibition on the taking of private property without just compensation. They asked the court to block future use of their father’s likeness on license plates and registration tags.Their argument centered on whether an intangible asset, such as a trademark or a person’s likeness, can be treated as property protected by the Fifth Amendment. The family’s lawyers said the lower courts wrongly suggested that the amendment does not automatically apply to intangible property in the same way it applies to land or other tangible assets.The Clemente family warned that the lower court’s reasoning could allow governments to take trademarks without paying for them, subject only to a balancing test that could leave owners with little protection. They argued that such a rule would invite governments to appropriate valuable intellectual property on demand.Puerto Rico disputed that interpretation. In its filing to the Supreme Court, the territory said the First Circuit did not categorically exclude intangible property from Fifth Amendment protection, but instead applied existing precedent to the specific facts of the case.Why the courts sided with Puerto RicoA U.S. District Court judge in San Juan dismissed the case, finding that Puerto Rico was immune from the lawsuit. The First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston later partially affirmed that dismissal, rejecting the family’s claim that Puerto Rico’s use of the trademark amounted to an unconstitutional taking.The appeals court also ruled that the Clemente family could not sue under the Fifth Amendment for intangible property such as a trademark. That conclusion was central to the case, because it meant the family could not pursue the damages they sought through that constitutional theory.Puerto Rico’s lawyers argued that the Supreme Court had no reason to intervene. They said the lower courts had followed established precedent and that there was no conflict among lower courts on the legal questions raised by the Clemente family.The Supreme Court agreed, declining to hear the case without comment. That decision does not create a new precedent, but it leaves the First Circuit’s ruling in place and closes the family’s path to a Supreme Court review in this dispute.Clemente’s enduring legacyRoberto Clemente remains one of baseball’s most admired figures, both for his performance on the field and for his humanitarian work. He played 18 seasons for the Pittsburgh Pirates from 1955 to 1972, earning 15 All-Star selections and winning two World Series titles.He was the World Series MVP in 1971 and finished his career with a .317 batting average, 3,000 hits, 1,305 RBIs and 240 home runs. The Baseball Hall of Fame inducted him posthumously in 1973, waiving its usual five-year waiting period.Clemente died at age 38 on December 31, 1972, in a plane crash while delivering humanitarian aid to earthquake victims in Nicaragua. His death transformed him into a symbol of service and sacrifice, and his legacy remains deeply meaningful in Puerto Rico and across baseball.What the decision meansThe Supreme Court’s decision does not erase Clemente’s legacy or diminish the emotional weight of the dispute. It simply means that Puerto Rico will not face a federal constitutional trial over its use of the image on commemorative plates.For the Clemente family, the outcome is a legal setback, but it also highlights the ongoing challenge of protecting a loved one’s name and likeness after death. For Puerto Rico, it confirms that the state can honor a cultural icon through public programs without facing the constitutional claim the family pursued.The case may end in the courts, but the broader question it raised remains relevant. As governments increasingly use images, names and symbols to commemorate public figures, the line between a tribute and an unauthorized commercial use can become difficult to define.You use AI every day. articles.title: After NEET row, NTA invites retired defence personnel to monitor exams
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The National Testing Agency (NTA) is planning a permanent pool of independent examination observers, including retired armed forces and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The National Testing Agency (NTA) is planning a permanent pool of independent examination observers, including retired armed forces and paramilitary personnel and retired government officers, as part of efforts to strengthen examination security following the NEET-UG paper leak controversy.The observer's role is separate from and in addition to that of the city coordinator and centre superintendent, with a direct reporting line to the NTA."To meet the requirement in a timely and reliable manner across an annual examination cycle, NTA proposes to build and maintain a standing, pre-verified pool of empanelled Observers, drawn from retired and serving academic and administrative staff of government institutions," the EOI document said.The agency has invited applications under three categories: retired Central and state government officers; retired armed forces and paramilitary personnel; and retired or serving teachers and professors from government schools, colleges and universities.For examination centres located outside India, the NTA will ordinarily empanel observers from among Indian nationals residing in the same city.NTA sets infrastructure norms for exam centresSeparately, the NTA has invited institutions and organisations that own, operate or have legally enforceable use-rights over suitable facilities to apply for empanelment as examination centres.For computer-based tests (CBT), applicants are required to have 285 fully functional computer workstations, including buffer capacity, per shift.For pen-and-paper tests (PPT), a minimum of 250 candidate seats, including buffer capacity, per shift is required.CBT centres must have at least four separate computer labs or halls, each with 30 workstations. For PPT examinations, centres must have at least six separate halls accommodating 40 candidates each, or equivalent configurations.The initiatives come amid efforts to overhaul the national examination system following the NEET-UG paper leak controversy, which triggered nationwide student protests and raised questions about the security and integrity of competitive examinations.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'US fabricating spy narratives to impose tech blockade': China on Nvidia CEO row
articles.summary: China hit back at US over allegations linking an alleged Chinese spy to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, accusing Washington of fabricating a spying narrative to
articles.body: China hit back at US over allegations linking an alleged Chinese spy to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, accusing Washington of fabricating a spying narrative to justify imposing a technological blockade.“China urges the US to stop fabricating so-called spy narratives and using them as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade,” foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular briefing on Thursday, as quoted by Reuters.She added that China's scientific and technological progress was driven by independent innovation and open cooperation. Beijing was also willing to work with Washington to implement the consensus reached by the two countries' leaders, she added.The latest remarks come amid growing scrutiny of Nvidia and its chief executive Jensen Huang after reports linked him to Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence officials of working for Beijing. The allegations have not been independently verified by Reuters.Meanwhile, Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The CEO admitted in a message to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, but did not name the woman. He has said he would cooperate with the probe and reaffirmed his commitment to US national security. Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe that national security information or company trade secrets were compromised.Beijing had rejected the espionage allegations earlier this week as well. On Monday, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the claims “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
